There is the possibility of IP/session data leakage if someone is able to sniff TURN traffic, but honestly, if an actor is able to do so, they will be able to see the source and destination IPs of all traffic anyway, so encrypting the TURN traffic doesn't give you anything.\r\n\r\nIn my experience, an encrypted connection to the TURN server was required because of proxy/firewall rules on a particular client network, not because of the risk of MITM at the TURN server. class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">Perhaps I misunderstood something as well, but <code class="notranslate">--no_tcp</code> + <code class="notranslate">--no_udp</code> should break coTURN functionality completely, since it must either communicate via TCP or UDP or both?</p>
<p dir="auto">I as well found no way to disable <code class="notranslate">listening-port</code> (non TLS) at all. If not defined, it will use the default port <code class="notranslate">3478</code>. Would be great if we had an option to only listen to the <code class="notranslate">tls-listening-port</code> via TLS.</p>
<p dir="auto">However it is still possible to ensure encrypted TURN connections:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>In the mentioned case with Nextcloud, one can anyway only configure one specific port in the Talk app settings, so if the assigned TLS port is entered there, all Nextcloud Talk connections will be TLS encrypted.</li>
<li>Of course other clients can still use coTURN via unencrypted port. To handle this:
<ul dir="auto">
<li>In case behind a NAT, simply only forward the TLS port.</li>
<li>If you want to block non-TLS also within local network or coTURN is not behind a NAT, use <code class="notranslate">iptables</code>/<code class="notranslate">nftables</code> (respectively whatever firewall) to block the non-TLS port (+ alternative <code class="notranslate">alt-listening-port</code>, which is by default <code class="notranslate">listening-port</code>+1 = <code class="notranslate">3479</code>), or at best block all ports besides the required ones.</li>
</ul>
</li>

<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Tls and plain as the config files says are listening also on the other Port.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Okay this would be indeed a bug or a totally unreasonable confusing behaviour and security issue. Already the <code class="notranslate">alt-</code>* ports that are listened to by default don't make much sense to me. Either the ONE port works, or it doesn't and should be fixed, or if for any reason required, one could be allowed to "explicitly" add multiple ports.</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">This can be configured.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">What you mean? You can change the above behaviour?</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">The nextcloud Check responded without Error with no-tcp and no-udp enabled.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Hmm, I am no specialist, but that does not make much sense to me either. What I could think of, is that disabling both is simply ignored, as this would break functionality completely? Or how should coTURN communicate aside with TCP or UDP?</p>
<hr>
<p dir="auto">Okay I read the config file comments about this. coTURN listens to both (all) ports the exact same way and automatically determines plain or TLS connection.<br>
But "<code class="notranslate">if allowed by configuration</code>"? So how to deny this?</p>
<p dir="auto">Further:</p>
<div class="snippet-clipboard-content notranslate position-relative overflow-auto" data-snippet-clipboard-copy-content="# Uncomment if no UDP client listener is desired.

<ul dir="auto">
<li>So does this mean that <code class="notranslate">no-udp/tcp</code> explicitly means plain (non-D/TLS) connections?</li>
<li>I am no specialist, but (D)TLS connections are still wrapped into TCP or UDP! Definitely confusing.</li>
<li>Better/clearer to me would be: <code class="notranslate">no-udp/tcp</code> meaning indeed that for plain and TLS connections either UDP or TCP is disabled. And having <code class="notranslate">no-tls/plain</code> instead to disable encrypted or unencrypted listener.</li>
<li>And of course this should not only stop listening to the ports (as long as they can be used for both), but block TLS/non-TLS connections completely then.</li>

data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">No, even with an unencrypted connection with the TURN server, the WebRTC data cannot be compromised. Key exchange in WebRTC is done on a different layer (often called the signaling layer), and it is the signaling layer that needs to be encrypted and secure to prevent snooping or MITM attacks.</p>
<p dir="auto">The TURN server is just a relay, it has no knowledge or insight into the data being send back and forth between WebRTC peers; all it sees are data packets that come from client A which need to be sent to client B. There is the possibility of IP/session data leakage if someone is able to sniff TURN traffic, but honestly, if an actor is able to do so, they will be able to see the source and destination IPs of all traffic anyway, so encrypting the TURN traffic doesn't give you anything.</p>
<p dir="auto">In my experience, an encrypted connection to the TURN server was required because of proxy/firewall rules on a particular client network, not because of the risk of MITM at the TURN server. If your configuration works without (D)TLS to the TURN server, then there's no reason to enforce it.</p>
<p dir="auto">TL;DR make your signaling layer is encrypted and secure, don't bother with (D)TLS on the TURN server unless you really need to.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" Don't use TLS/DTLS listeners

This is not supported by Nextcloud Talk and it's also not required for
WebRTC because traffic is already encrypted on a different layer.

See the following issues for details:

https://github.com/coturn/coturn/issues/33
https://github.com/nextcloud/spreed/issues/257

Quoting a comment by @bradleythughes from the first issue:

> No, even with an unencrypted connection with the TURN server, the
> WebRTC data cannot be compromised. Key exchange in WebRTC is done on a
> different layer (often called the signaling layer), and it is the
> signaling layer that needs to be encrypted and secure to prevent
> snooping or MITM attacks.
>
> The TURN server is just a relay, it has no knowledge or insight into
> the data being send back and forth between WebRTC peers; all it sees
> are data packets that come from client A which need to be sent to
> client B. There is the possibility of IP/session data leakage if
> someone is able to sniff TURN traffic, but honestly, if an actor is
> able to do so, they will be able to see the source and destination IPs
> of all traffic anyway, so encrypting the TURN traffic doesn't give you
> anything.
>
> In my experience, an encrypted connection to the TURN server was
> required because of proxy/firewall rules on a particular client
> network, not because of the risk of MITM at the TURN server. If your
> configuration works without (D)TLS to the TURN server, then there's no
> reason to enforce it.
>
> TL;DR make your signaling layer is encrypted and secure, don't bother
> with (D)TLS on the TURN server unless you really need to.

<li>
<p dir="auto">coTURN ALWAYS listens to four ports:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li><code class="notranslate">listening-port</code> (default = <code class="notranslate">3478</code>)</li>
<li><code class="notranslate">tls-listening-port</code> (default = <code class="notranslate">5349</code>)</li>
<li><code class="notranslate">alt-listening-port</code> (default = <code class="notranslate">listening-port + 1</code>)</li>
<li><code class="notranslate">alt-tls-listening-port</code> (default = <code class="notranslate">tls-listening-port + 1</code>)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto">It generally allows (D)TLS and plain connections on all four ports.</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>You can limit to plain via <code class="notranslate">no-(d)tls</code> or let it fail by adding no <code class="notranslate">cert</code>/<code class="notranslate">pkey</code>.</li>
<li>You can limit to (D)TLS via <code class="notranslate">no-udp</code> + <code class="notranslate">no-tcp</code></li>
<li>You can combine the above to limit to any combination of (plain) UDP, (pain) TCP, TLS or DTLS.</li>
<li>Finally you can limit the TLS protocol via <code class="notranslate">no-tlsv1</code>, <code class="notranslate">no-tlsv1_1</code> and/or <code class="notranslate">no-tlsv1_2</code></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto"><strong>But what ever you allow via above, it always applies to all four ports!</strong></p>
</li>
</ul>
</blockquote>

<p dir="auto">Check <a href="https://github.com/coturn/coturn/blob/master/examples/run_tests.sh">https://github.com/coturn/coturn/blob/master/examples/run_tests.sh</a> for the shared_secret usage that uses time limited TURN credentials. You can check this doc for the explaination of how it works: <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-uberti-behave-turn-rest-00" rel="nofollow">https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-uberti-behave-turn-rest-00</a></p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Sorry for bumping an old issue, but just so have I understood it correctly:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>If unencrypted TURN is being used (no cert or --no-tls + --no-dtls) username:passwords will be sent in plaintext to the TURN server.
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Therefore do <strong>not</strong> use lt-cred-mech and <em>static</em> user:password when running unencrypted</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>If using use-auth-secret, the static-auth-secret is never sent at all (plaintext or not) to authenticate, instead its used to generate ephermal user:password pairs - which are sent in plaintext in the case of unencrypted TURN.</li>
<li>Encrypting TURN (TURNS) encrypts these user:password pairs, but also encrypts WebRTC data <em>again</em>.</li>
<li>WebRTC data is always encrypted independent of turns: or turn:</li>
</ul>
<p dir="auto">What is the scope of things an MITM could do if the TURN is using use-auth-secret? The MITM can see all user:password pairs but what is the damage that can be done? Just a DoS? Use the turn server for DDoS attacks? But the WebRTC data (VoIP) is still protected, that is not compromised by nor can be trough knowing authentication to the TURN server.</p>
<p dir="auto">Is there any way to send the TURN authentication encrypted (with turns:) but <em>not</em> re-encrypt the WebRTC data?</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions"
